learningObjectives.title: Modern warfare and its impact on society (c1900-present)

questions.q: Which weapon gave English armies a major advantage at battles such as Crecy and Agincourt?
options: The longbow
The musket
The machine gun
The bayonet
questions.explain: The longbow could fire rapidly over long range and was decisive in English victories at Crecy (1346) and Agincourt (1415).

questions.q: In which year was the Battle of Agincourt fought?
questions.explain: Agincourt was fought in 1415, with English longbowmen defeating a much larger French force.

questions.q: Under the medieval feudal system, why could a king raise an army from his nobles?
options: Nobles owed military service in return for the land granted to them
Nobles were paid a national wage by the state
All men were conscripted by law
Soldiers were hired from foreign mercenary firms only
questions.explain: Feudal landholding obliged nobles and their knights to provide military service to the king in exchange for land.

questions.q: Why did the spread of gunpowder weapons reduce the importance of the mounted armoured knight?
options: Firearms and cannon could pierce armour and break up cavalry charges
Knights were banned by royal decree
Horses became too expensive to breed
Knights refused to fight in castles
questions.explain: Gunpowder weapons could penetrate plate armour and destroy fortifications, making the heavily armoured mounted knight far less dominant.

questions.q: The New Model Army, created in 1645, is most closely associated with which Parliamentarian leader?
options: Oliver Cromwell
The Duke of Wellington
Horatio Nelson
Edward Cardwell
questions.explain: The New Model Army of the English Civil War is strongly associated with Oliver Cromwell, who commanded its cavalry and later led Parliament.

questions.q: What made the New Model Army different from earlier English armies?
options: It was a professional, full-time, paid national force with promotion by merit
It relied entirely on feudal levies of unpaid peasants
It used only longbows and refused firearms
It was made up solely of foreign mercenaries
questions.explain: The New Model Army was a disciplined, professionally organised and paid national force in which officers could be promoted on ability rather than birth.

questions.q: A 14th-century English commander facing a French cavalry charge on muddy ground would most rely on which tactic?
options: Positioning longbowmen behind defensive stakes
Forming infantry into a hollow bayonet square
Digging deep trenches with machine-gun nests
Massing artillery for a creeping barrage
questions.explain: English commanders used protected longbowmen behind stakes to break up cavalry, as seen at Agincourt where mud slowed the French charge.

questions.q: In which year was the Battle of Waterloo fought?
questions.explain: The Battle of Waterloo was fought in 1815, when the Duke of Wellington's forces defeated Napoleon.

questions.q: At Waterloo in 1815, British infantry facing a charge by French cavalry would most likely respond by doing what?
options: Forming a defensive infantry square
Charging forward on horseback
Digging protective trench lines
Retreating into a stone castle
questions.explain: Infantry formed squares bristling with bayonets so cavalry could not break through, a standard tactic at Waterloo.

questions.q: What was the nickname of the standard British infantry musket used through much of the 18th and early 19th centuries?
options: The Brown Bess
The Minie
The Maxim
The Baker square
questions.explain: The smoothbore Land Pattern musket, nicknamed the Brown Bess, was the standard British infantry firearm for over a century.

questions.q: Why did line infantry of this period fight using massed volley fire?
options: Muskets were inaccurate, so firing in mass maximised the chance of hits
Each soldier could accurately snipe individual targets
Ammunition was unlimited and cheap
It allowed soldiers to remain hidden in cover
questions.explain: Smoothbore muskets were inaccurate at range, so disciplined ranks firing simultaneous volleys were used to produce effective concentrated fire.

questions.q: Which nurse became famous for improving conditions for wounded soldiers during the Crimean War?
options: Florence Nightingale
Emmeline Pankhurst
Elizabeth I
Boudicca
questions.explain: Florence Nightingale reformed the care of wounded soldiers at Scutari during the Crimean War (1853-56).

questions.q: What was a key impact of reports from the Crimean War on the British army?
options: They exposed poor conditions and led to improvements in military medicine and sanitation
They ended the use of firearms in the army
They abolished the navy
They introduced the longbow once more
questions.explain: Publicity about disease and neglect in the Crimea drove reforms in army medical care, hygiene and hospital organisation.

questions.q: The Cardwell reforms of the 1870s abolished the purchase of commissions. What was the main aim of this change?
options: To base officer selection on merit rather than wealth
To make the army entirely voluntary and unpaid
To replace rifles with muskets
To hand command of the army to Parliament directly
questions.explain: Ending the buying of commissions in 1871 aimed to make the officer corps more professional and based on ability rather than the ability to pay.

questions.q: A mid-19th-century soldier issued a Minie rifle instead of a smoothbore musket would gain what main advantage?
options: Greater range and accuracy of fire
A lighter weapon that never needed reloading
The ability to fire without gunpowder
Protection from cavalry without forming a square
questions.explain: Rifled weapons such as the Minie rifle spun the bullet, giving far greater range and accuracy than smoothbore muskets.

questions.q: In which year was conscription first introduced in Britain during the First World War?
questions.explain: The Military Service Act introduced conscription in Britain in 1916 as volunteer numbers proved insufficient.

questions.q: At which 1916 battle were tanks used in warfare for the first time?
options: The Battle of the Somme
The Battle of Waterloo
The Battle of Agincourt
The Battle of Naseby
questions.explain: Britain first deployed tanks during the Battle of the Somme in 1916, though they were unreliable at this early stage.

questions.q: Why did the Western Front in the First World War develop into a stalemate of trench warfare?
options: Machine guns and artillery gave a huge advantage to defenders
Cavalry charges could easily break enemy lines
Neither side had any modern weapons
Soldiers refused to leave the trenches at all
questions.explain: Rapid-firing machine guns and heavy artillery made attacks across open ground extremely costly, favouring defence and producing trench stalemate.

questions.q: What does the term 'total war' mean in the context of the modern conflicts on the specification?
options: The whole nation's population and economy are mobilised and civilians are directly affected
Wars fought only by professional soldiers far from home
Conflicts in which no weapons are used
Battles limited to a single day
questions.explain: Total war mobilises an entire society, so civilians face rationing, bombing and war work as well as soldiers at the front.

questions.q: During the Second World War, to protect civilians from German bombing raids the British government organised which measure?
options: Evacuation of children from cities to the countryside
Training civilians to use the longbow
Raising a feudal levy of knights
Forming infantry into defensive squares
questions.explain: Facing air raids such as the Blitz, the government evacuated children from cities to safer rural areas to reduce civilian casualties.
